entities.name: Aelianus Tacticus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Aelianus Tacticus, a Greek military writer flourishing around 100-200 CE, established himself in Rome as a significant compiler and interpreter of Hellenistic military theory. His singular extant work, *On Tactical Formations of the Greeks* (Περὶ ἐν τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τάξεων), stands as a critical primary source for understanding the intricacies of the Macedonian phalanx and Greek drill. Rather than an experienced field commander, Aelianus was a scholarly theorist, dedicated to preserving and systematizing the tactical knowledge of previous Greek strategists, particularly those associated with Alexander the Great and his Hellenistic successors. His work emerged during a period when the Roman Empire, while militarily dominant, still valued and integrated aspects of Greek intellectual tradition.

The treatise itself is a detailed, prescriptive manual describing the organization, movements, and command structure of a Hellenistic infantry phalanx. Aelianus meticulously outlines the various formations, commands, and evolutions, providing precise dimensions for ranks and files, and even specifying the roles of different officers. He explicitly states his intention to provide a theoretical model for Emperor Trajan, although it is debated whether his work was ever practically implemented by Roman legions, which relied on their distinct cohort system. Nevertheless, *On Tactical Formations* offered a comprehensive, almost mathematical, exposition of a military system that had dominated the Eastern Mediterranean for centuries.
